cards.text: This one's a psalm of Asaph, the chief of the Levites King David appointed to praise the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). And Asaph skips the small talk. No hello, no how's the weather, he cries out to God, OUT LOUD, so God will hear him.
In the day of trouble, Asaph seeks the Lord. All through the night his hands stay outstretched, and they don't grow weary.

cards.question: In his day of trouble, how does Asaph's soul respond to comfort?

cards.text: So Asaph turns his thoughts to God Himself, right there in the middle of his trouble.

cards.question: When Asaph remembers God in his trouble, what happens to him?

answers.text: He groans and his spirit grows faint
He sings and his spirit grows strong
He rests and his spirit grows calm

cards.text: And sleep? Asaph tells God He's kept his eyes from closing, so now Asaph's up all night, lying there, supervising the ceiling.

cards.question: Up all night, Asaph is so ___ that he can't even speak.

cards.text: So Asaph thinks back to the days of old, the years long in the past. At night he remembers his song, and his spirit starts asking some hard questions.

cards.question: In the night, Asaph's spirit starts asking hard questions. What does he ask might go on forever?

answers.text: The Lord turning away from His people
His own nights without any sleep

cards.question: In his questions, Asaph even wonders if God's promise has failed for all time.
Asaph wonders if God has forgotten to be gracious. Deep down, he's asking if God has stopped showing ___.
After all those questions, Asaph sums up his grief in one line. What does he say has changed?

answers.text: The right hand of the Most High
The hearts of the people of Israel
The song he sang in the night

cards.text: Then the whole psalm turns on one little word: will. Asaph quits supervising the ceiling and finally flips on the light.

cards.question: After all his hard questions, Asaph decides to ___ the works of the LORD.
Asaph plans to take a quick glance at what God has done and move right along.

cards.text: Asaph tells God that His way is holy.

cards.question: Right after calling God's way holy, Asaph asks God a question. Which one?

answers.text: What god is so great as our God
How long will this night go on
Why have You left us all alone

cards.text: He calls God the One who works wonders and shows His strength among the peoples. Ten verses ago this man was too troubled to talk, and now he's the loudest guy in the STADIUM.

cards.question: Asaph says God redeemed His people with power. Who are they?

answers.text: The sons of Jacob and Joseph
The sons of Moab and Ammon
The sons of Esau and Ishmael

cards.text: Now Asaph stops talking about God's wonders and starts painting one. And it starts with water.

cards.question: In Asaph's picture, what do the waters do when they see God?

answers.text: They swirl and even the depths shake
They freeze and the depths stand still
They rise and cover the whole land

cards.text: Then the sky joins in: clouds pour down water, thunder resounds, and God's arrows flash back and forth. I bet it sounded like every oven door in my bakery slamming shut at ONCE.

cards.question: With God's thunder resounding in the whirlwind, the earth stays perfectly still.

cards.text: The lightning lights up the world, and the earth trembles and quakes. Meanwhile me? I used to jump when somebody rattled the junk drawer looking for TAPE.

cards.question: God's path led through the sea, His way through the mighty waters, and His footprints were plain for anyone to see.

cards.text: A path you can walk, but no footprints you can find. I think that's Asaph's whole long night in one line: God was at work even when Asaph couldn't see a trace of Him.

cards.question: God's footprints can't be found, but He still leads. How does He lead His people?

answers.text: Like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron
Like an army by the hand of Joshua and Caleb
Like a nation by the hand of David and Solomon

cards.text: Moses and Aaron, the two the LORD told to bring the Israelites out of Egypt (Exodus 6:26). The man who was once too troubled to speak ends this psalm remembering God leading His people like a flock.

findings.problem: Psalm 77:9 says God's 'compassion,' not 'mercy.' The right answer swaps in a different word. 'Deep down, he's asking' also states, as fact, what Asaph really means. The second question in the verse ('Has His anger shut off His compassion?') is turned into a paraphrase, and its wording is never actually told.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: 'The whole psalm turns on one little word: will' is not true as stated. 'Will' already opens Asaph's despairing question in Psalm 77:7 ('Will the Lord spurn us forever'), so the word itself is not what marks the turn.

rule.text: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: 'Asaph tells God that His way is holy.' is a flat restatement with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a stripped-down summary.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The question says Asaph 'asks God a question.' But Psalm 77:13's question refers to God in the third person ('What god is so great as our God?'), so the text leaves open who is being asked.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The wrong answer 'Why have You left us all alone' is close to what Asaph does ask in Psalm 77:7 ('Will the Lord spurn us forever...?'). A baker could argue Asaph asks something like it in this passage.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: The card ties Psalm 77:19 to Asaph's sleepless night and states that 'God was at work even when Asaph couldn't see a trace of Him.' The text never makes that connection; 'I think' marks an opinion but doesn't make the connection allowed. 'A path you can walk' also adds to 'Your path led through the sea.' The card cites only 77:19 but draws on 77:2-6.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The second sentence ('The man who was once too troubled to speak ends this psalm remembering God leading His people like a flock') only recaps Psalm 77:20, which card 15 already answered, plus the psalm's arc. It doesn't move the passage forward.
